value.text: In July 2025, the White House released “Winning the AI Race: America’s AI Action Plan,” which it described as identifying over 90 federal policy actions across innovation, infrastructure, and international diplomacy and security. In March 2026, the White House issued a national AI legislative framework and said it looked forward to working with Congress to turn the framework into legislation. A September 2026 executive order directed executive-branch departments and agencies to use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” instead of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” in official communications. A June 2026 executive order promoted advanced AI innovation and security, including a voluntary framework with AI developers, while stating that one section did not authorize mandatory government licensing, preclearance, or permitting for new AI models.

A June 2026 executive order promoted advanced AI innovation and security, including a voluntary framework with AI developers, while stating that one section did not authorize mandatory government licensing, preclearance, or permitting for new AI models.

value.text: NIST released the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) as voluntary guidance for organizations to manage AI risks and pursue benefits while reducing negative impacts. NIST has described its AI work as including measurement and evaluation, technical standards, and contributions to AI policy, and it serves as the federal AI standards coordinator. In 2025, NIST’s CAISI evaluated PRC-developed AI models and reported that they lagged behind U.S. models in performance, cost, security, and adoption. NIST announced an AI Agent Standards Initiative aimed at fostering industry-led technical standards and secure, interoperable adoption of AI agents.

value.text: OMB's March 2024 memorandum directed agencies to advance AI governance and innovation while managing risks, including minimum risk management practices for AI uses affecting public rights and safety. That memorandum required agencies to submit plans or written determinations to OMB and post them publicly, and to inventory AI use cases at least annually, submit the inventory to OMB, and post a public version. OMB later rescinded and replaced M-24-10 with M-25-21 and issued M-25-22 guidance to agencies on acquiring AI responsibly. A December 2025 OMB memorandum required agencies to include contractual requirements addressing compliance with the Unbiased AI Principles in post-date LLM procurement solicitations or orders, and listed truth-seeking LLMs as a principle.

That memorandum required agencies to submit plans or written determinations to OMB and post them publicly, and to inventory AI use cases at least annually, submit the inventory to OMB, and post a public version.
OMB later rescinded and replaced M-24-10 with M-25-21 and issued M-25-22 guidance to agencies on acquiring AI responsibly.

A December 2025 OMB memorandum required agencies to include contractual requirements addressing compliance with the Unbiased AI Principles in post-date LLM procurement solicitations or orders, and listed truth-seeking LLMs as a principle.

The Department has described AI governance measures, including strengthened governance bodies and implementation at executive, strategic, tactical, and operational levels, and it developed a Risk Management Profile for AI and Human Rights with NIST and USAID.

Its supplied statements also describe international AI frameworks and cooperation, including endorsed rules for responsible military AI use, a UN General Assembly resolution on safe, secure, and trustworthy AI, and a G7 multilateral framework for advanced AI developers.

value.text: Hegseth described responsible AI at the War Department as objectively truthful capabilities used securely and within governing laws, and said the department will not employ models that won't allow it to fight wars. He announced an AI acceleration strategy and the GenAI.mil platform, including Google Gemini and xAI's Grok, and urged department members to incorporate AI into their workflows. He also said the department will invest in AI compute and run experimentation campaigns, aiming to become an AI-first warfighting force.

value.text: In June 2026 remarks, Ratcliffe said that when he became Director he made emerging technologies a top priority alongside China, and that CIA must excel in AI because algorithmic decisions and data affect U.S. strategic advantage and national security. He described frontier AI capabilities as akin to “digital nuclear weapons” and said the U.S. cannot afford to wait for a risk-free approach to emerging technology, must move fast and aggressively, and must master technology better than adversaries who seek to steal and manipulate American advancements. He also said widespread AI adoption is transforming CIA business and that advances in AI, quantum, and biotech are rewriting conflict, with AI-powered robots and drones potentially having devastating battlefield lethality. In a January 2025 statement, Ratcliffe said AI and machine learning can help the intelligence community find the signal in large volumes of data and spend more time using intelligence.

value.text: DHS’s September 2025 AI Strategy outlines a three-year approach to removing barriers to responsible AI use, enhancing AI maturity, and ensuring transparency and accountability to the public. value.text: On January 25, 2024, the FTC announced 6(b) orders to five companies seeking information about investments and partnerships involving generative AI companies and major cloud service providers. The FTC has described using existing legal authorities and Section 5 to address deceptive or unfair AI-related practices, including AI claims and schemes. In 2026, the FTC proposed a policy statement on applying Section 5’s deceptive-practices prohibition to companies marketing AI systems, including concerns about steering AI outputs away from user expectations. The FTC also said it intends to study how companies offering AI companions monetize user engagement and protect children online.

value.text: Nick Andersen said CISA would roll out specific artificial intelligence platform access for federal government-wide partners before the end of the week. In May 2025 congressional testimony, Andersen said designating technologies such as cloud computing and AI companies as critical infrastructure could allow examination of minimum cybersecurity requirements and greater information sharing.

value.text: In an April 2024 posture statement, General Eric M. Smith said the Marine Corps is leveraging AI, robotics, and commercial technology as part of the Department of Defense’s Replicator Initiative (s1), and he described Replicator as an opportunity to accelerate modernization if managed carefully (s2). In other posture statements, Smith described integrating AI with sensors and targeting systems to improve sensing and precision fires (s3), and moving to an increment that adds edge-based AI and electronic warfare capabilities (s4). In a May 2026 statement, Smith said Dynamis enables AI-powered decision advantage by integrating commercial technologies with Marine Corps warfighting functions (s5), and that MSS, used by over 4,900 Marines, reflects leveraging AI to shape decision-making and improve kill-chain capabilities (s6). In January 2025, Smith said the Marine Corps would not reorganize based on AI but would use available tools (s7); in May 2025 he described expanding AI-driven adaptive learning in education and training (s12, s13) and stated that there is always a human on the loop (s15).

value.text: Daniel Glad said companies cannot claim mature AI governance or serious antitrust compliance without examining whether AI tools facilitate competitor coordination and understanding how pricing technology works. He said antitrust rules do not change when conduct moves to software, that software cannot launder collusion, and that Sherman Act accountability remains for corporations and individuals. He described the key question as whether there is an agreement among competitors, regardless of whether the hub is a spreadsheet, platform, or large language model, and said detection capability grows as conduct migrates to software because automated bids, data inputs, and queries leave records. He said the Whistleblower Rewards Program is well-positioned for AI and algorithmic risks and identified software platforms that aggregate competitor data and return pricing recommendations as the most developed area of algorithmic antitrust enforcement.
